(CNN) -- Tens of thousands of Congolese refugees fled camps Tuesday in the Democratic Republic of Congo as rebel troops attacked government forces in the area, the U.N. refugee agency said. Refugees move along a road Tuesday in Mugunga, near Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A press release from the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said it didn't appear rebels had targeted the camps, but it reported some were looted after camp residents, classified as internally displaced persons, fled. Roads to Goma, about 10 miles from the camps, were crowded with refugees and local residents fleeing the fighting, the UNHCR reported. Torrential rain made the movement even more difficult. "The main road toward Sake was crowded with people; we had difficulties getting through," UNHCR field safety adviser Pierre Nazroo was quoted as saying in the agency's release. "Internally displaced people are moving from site to site, direction Goma." UNHCR spokesman Ron Redmond said, "They have been living in extremely difficult conditions anyway. Now they have nothing but what they can carry." Redmond added, "These are people in poor health; they are soaking wet because of the torrential downpours. They need shelter, they need water, they need a lot of assistance so we're going to have to move quickly to get that help to them because a lot of them are already in a weakened state." While the Congolese government accused troops under rebel general Laurent Nkunda of staging the attack, a Nkunda spokesman denied the allegation, according to a report from the Integrated Regional Information Networks, a U.N.-affiliated news service. The spokesman, Bwambale Kakolele, said Rwandan Hutu rebels who also operate in the area were behind the attack, that report said. A spokesman for the U.N. military mission in the Congo said it was uncertain which group attacked the Congo army outpost near the village of Kishangazi, according to the U.N.-affiliated news service. "We think it could have been insurgents close to Nkunda who attacked, but we cannot rule out the [Rwandan rebels]," spokesman Col. Pierre Cherayron was quoted as saying. The UNHCR identified the affected camps as Mugunga I, Mugunga II, Lac Vert and Bulengo, saying about 28,000 had abandoned the first three camps and about 2,000 had left Bulengo. The UNHCR said 375,000 Congolese in North Kivu province have been forced from their homes in the past year. In the past two months alone, 160,000 have fled their homes amid the fighting between renegade troops and government forces, the agency said. North Kivu is in eastern Congo near the borders of Rwanda and Uganda. Congolese President Joseph Kabila has tried to gain a cease-fire with the rebels in the area under Nkunda, but fighting continues as hard-liners among the rebels and in the government have blocked reconciliation efforts, according to the International Crisis Group, an nongovernmental organization looking for solutions to conflicts. outputs.L2:
(CNN) — The U.N. refugee agency said Tuesday that tens of thousands of Congolese refugees left camps in the Democratic Republic of Congo after rebel forces attacked government troops nearby.

On Tuesday, refugees were seen traveling along a road in Mugunga, close to Goma in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

In a statement, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said the camps did not appear to have been the rebels’ intended targets. However, the agency said some camps were looted after residents—described as internally displaced people—ran away.

According to UNHCR, roads leading to Goma, roughly 10 miles from the camps, were packed with refugees and local people escaping the violence. Heavy rain made the journey even harder.

“The main road toward Sake was crowded with people; we had difficulties getting through,” UNHCR field safety adviser Pierre Nazroo said in the agency’s statement. “Internally displaced people are moving from site to site, direction Goma.”

UNHCR spokesman Ron Redmond said the displaced people had already been living in extremely harsh circumstances. “Now they have nothing but what they can carry,” he said.

Redmond also said many of them were in poor physical condition and were drenched because of the intense rainstorms. “They need shelter, they need water, they need a lot of assistance so we’re going to have to move quickly to get that help to them because a lot of them are already in a weakened state,” he said.

The Congolese government blamed troops loyal to rebel general Laurent Nkunda for the attack. However, a spokesman for Nkunda rejected that accusation, according to a report by the Integrated Regional Information Networks, a U.N.-affiliated news service.

That spokesman, Bwambale Kakolele, said the assault was carried out by Rwandan Hutu rebels, who are also active in the region, the report said.

A spokesman for the U.N. military mission in Congo said it was not yet clear which armed group had attacked the Congolese army post near the village of Kishangazi, according to the U.N.-linked news service.

“We think it could have been insurgents close to Nkunda who attacked, but we cannot rule out the [Rwandan rebels],” spokesman Col. Pierre Cherayron was quoted as saying.

UNHCR named the affected camps as Mugunga I, Mugunga II, Lac Vert and Bulengo. The agency said around 28,000 people had left the first three camps, while approximately 2,000 had departed Bulengo.

The agency also reported that 375,000 Congolese people in North Kivu province had been driven from their homes over the past year. In just the last two months, 160,000 people had fled because of clashes between renegade soldiers and government forces, UNHCR said.

North Kivu lies in eastern Congo, near the borders with Rwanda and Uganda.

Congolese President Joseph Kabila has attempted to secure a cease-fire with rebels in the area who are under Nkunda’s command. But the fighting has persisted, as hard-line factions among both the rebels and the government have obstructed reconciliation efforts, according to the International Crisis Group, a nongovernmental organization that works on conflict resolution.

**Tens of thousands flee displacement camps near Goma as fighting intensifies in eastern Congo**

**Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo** — Tens of thousands of internally displaced people have fled camps around the eastern Congolese city of Goma after renewed fighting between government forces and rebel groups in North Kivu province, according to the UN refugee agency.

The UNHCR said civilians who had already been uprooted by years of violence were once again on the move as clashes intensified near densely populated displacement sites on the outskirts of Goma, the provincial capital and a major humanitarian hub.

“Families who had sought safety in displacement camps are now being forced to flee again, often with nothing but the clothes they are wearing,” UNHCR said, warning that the latest movement of people is worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Fighting in North Kivu has escalated in recent weeks between the Congolese army and rebel forces, including the M23 movement, which has seized territory across parts of the province. The violence has pushed civilians toward Goma, a city already struggling to shelter and feed hundreds of thousands of displaced people.

UNHCR said displacement sites near Goma have come under increasing pressure, with families fleeing amid fears of shelling, armed incursions and deteriorating security. Many people are now sleeping in the open, along roadsides or in public buildings, with limited access to clean water, food and medical care.

“The humanitarian situation around Goma is extremely alarming,” the agency said. “Civilians must be protected, and displaced people must not be forced to move again because of insecurity in places where they have sought refuge.”

Aid agencies have warned that the collapse of basic services in displacement areas could fuel outbreaks of disease, particularly cholera and measles, which have previously spread rapidly in overcrowded camps around Goma.

Local residents described scenes of panic as families packed up bedding, cooking pots and plastic sheeting before leaving the camps. Some carried children on their backs while others pushed belongings on bicycles or wooden carts.

“We ran because the fighting was getting closer,” said one displaced woman who had fled a camp west of Goma. “We do not know where to go. We have already fled many times.”

The latest wave of displacement adds to one of the world’s largest and most neglected humanitarian crises. More than 6 million people are internally displaced across the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to UN estimates, with North Kivu among the worst-affected provinces.

UNHCR and partner organizations said they are working to provide emergency assistance, including shelter materials, protection services and basic relief items, but access remains constrained by insecurity and damaged roads.

The agency called on all parties to the conflict to respect international humanitarian law and ensure safe passage for civilians and aid workers.

“Those fleeing violence need urgent protection and assistance,” UNHCR said. “Without immediate support, the risks facing displaced families — especially women, children and older people — will only grow.”

The Congolese government has accused neighboring Rwanda of backing M23, an allegation Rwanda has repeatedly denied. The conflict has heightened regional tensions and prompted calls from the United Nations, African Union and regional leaders for a ceasefire and renewed diplomatic efforts.

For families fleeing the camps near Goma, however, the priority is immediate survival.

“We are tired of running,” another displaced man said. “Every time we find a place to stay, the war follows us.”

**UNHCR says eastern Congo camps emptied amid rebel advance**

**GENEVA/GOMA, Democratic Republic of Congo, Oct. 29** — Tens of thousands of displaced people have fled camps in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo after rebel attacks and fighting near the provincial capital, Goma, the U.N. refugee agency said, warning that civilians were again being driven deeper into a worsening humanitarian crisis.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said camps at Mugunga, Lac Vert and Bulengo, west of Goma in North Kivu province, had been abandoned as fighting intensified between Congolese government forces and rebels loyal to renegade Tutsi commander Laurent Nkunda.

UNHCR said its staff and aid partners were unable to determine immediately where many of the displaced had gone, but reports from the area suggested large numbers had fled toward Goma, surrounding villages or deeper into the bush. The agency expressed concern for people already uprooted by earlier waves of violence and now forced to flee again with little food, water or shelter.

The camps around Goma had housed civilians displaced by years of conflict in North Kivu, a mineral-rich province bordering Rwanda and Uganda. Aid agencies have repeatedly warned that renewed clashes in the region threaten to cut off assistance to vulnerable communities, including children, the elderly and survivors of sexual violence.

Nkunda, a former general in the Congolese army, leads the National Congress for the Defence of the People, or CNDP, a rebel movement that says it is protecting Congolese Tutsis from Rwandan Hutu militia members who fled into Congo after the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Congo’s government accuses Nkunda of seeking to carve out territory in the east and of receiving support from Rwanda, an allegation Kigali has denied.

The latest fighting has raised fears of a broader collapse around Goma, a city that became a focal point of regional conflict during Congo’s wars in the 1990s and early 2000s. Those wars drew in several neighbouring countries and left millions dead, most from hunger and disease.

Although Congo formally ended its last major war with a peace deal and elections, eastern provinces have remained unstable. Armed groups continue to compete for land, political influence and control of lucrative mineral trade routes, while the national army has struggled with poor discipline, weak command structures and accusations of abuses against civilians.

Humanitarian officials say North Kivu already had one of the largest displaced populations in Africa before the latest rebel offensive. Repeated fighting has left families moving from camp to camp, often returning briefly to their villages only to flee again when clashes resume.

UN agencies and relief groups have called for safe access to civilians and urged all parties to respect humanitarian law. Aid workers said the immediate priorities were to locate the displaced, restore water and sanitation services, and prevent outbreaks of disease among people sheltering in overcrowded areas or in the open.

The U.N. peacekeeping mission in Congo, known at the time as MONUC, has deployed forces in and around Goma but has faced criticism from residents who say it has failed to protect civilians from rebel advances and army reprisals. U.N. officials say peacekeepers are operating under difficult conditions and are seeking to prevent further attacks on populated areas.

The abandonment of the Mugunga, Lac Vert and Bulengo camps underscores the speed of the deterioration around Goma and the fragility of relief operations in a region where insecurity has repeatedly forced aid agencies to suspend distributions.

“This is a population that has already been displaced several times,” one humanitarian official said. “Every new round of fighting strips away what little people have managed to rebuild.”
